Internal Research  ·  Cambrian Network

Blockchain
oracles

How prices get on chain, and where they break

Why we looked at oracles
01

The bridge to off chain data

A blockchain is a closed system. A contract cannot read data that is off chain. For example, it does not know that ETH trades at $1,560 (or hopefully $6k).

Oracles are the bridge that brings outside information on chain. Since one of the main points of failure in lending protocols is the oracle, it earns a closer look.

The core problem

A contract that liquidates positions off a price feed is only as safe as that feed.

If the number is wrong, stale, or manipulable, the contract acts on a lie, and it has no way to know.

What an oracle is
02

The classic case is an asset price, but the same machinery could deliver proof that a stablecoin is backed, the outcome of a real world event, and so on.

Not the source, the layer
Queries, verifies, transmits
The oracle does not originate the data. It pulls from a source, checks it, and posts it on chain. If the source is wrong, the oracle relays a wrong number just as faithfully.
Sourcing and delivery are separate jobs
Sourcing is getting the raw data right, from the right markets, cleaned and aggregated. Delivery is putting it on chain reliably, fresh and cheap. A provider can be good at one and bad at the other, and most of the differences between providers come from this.
What a good oracle delivers
03
Correct
The value reflects reality, which depends on the quality and breadth of the sources.
Timely
Fresh enough for the case at hand. Lending tolerates more lag than a perpetuals exchange.
Hard to manipulate
An attacker cannot move the reported value cheaply, usually by pushing a thin source.

A contract cannot tell a wrong price from a right one. It acts on whatever the oracle reports. So the choice of oracle is a security decision.

Oracle types · push versus pull
04

Oracle designs are easiest to sort by how they deliver data, and what a protocol needs decides which fits. Lending tolerates lag for manipulation resistance, a perpetuals venue needs speed.

Push · written ahead of time
An external system writes prices on chain on a heartbeat or a deviation threshold. The contract just reads the latest value. Easy to integrate, but it can go stale silently if the updater stops.
Pull · written on demand
The price is signed off chain and only written when a consumer needs it, paying the gas. Very low latency, harder to integrate, and an unupdated feed fails rather than going stale.

Who pays and when: push reads are generally free. Pull consumers pay the gas each time the price is brought on chain, a cost the protocol can absorb.

Oracle extractable value
06

OEV is the value created at the moment an oracle updates. When an update reveals a liquidatable position, that value leaks to liquidation bots and block builders through gas wars, draining capital that could have stayed in the protocol.

$180M+
Paid to searchers · 2024 floor
Split
Protocol + oracle

The fix is to auction the right to run the triggering update, splitting the winning bid between protocol and oracle.

Pioneered by API3. Chainlink leads with Smart Value Recapture (Aave, Compound, Venus). RedStone runs its own.

Main providers
07

Three providers dominate. They differ mostly in how they source and deliver data, and in the markets they focus on.

Chainlink
By far the biggest, the default oracle for blue chip lending. Popularized push, secures more value across more protocols than anyone.
Pyth
The leading pull based provider. First party data, strongest in derivatives and non-EVM chains.
RedStone
Runs both push and pull across chains. Focused on yield bearing collateral for lending markets.
Chainlink
08

Each feed is updated by multiple independent node operators that report their observations. A contract aggregates them into a single value on chain, through its off chain reporting protocol.

The update rule is not a stream. A feed writes only when the price moves past a deviation threshold or when a heartbeat passes. A round can also require a minimum number of operators to respond.

Slow but reliable

It lags when prices move fast, but that is the price of being hard to manipulate, which is why big lending protocols rely on it.

Beyond the price feeds
Data Streams
Low latency pull style data for venues that need it, which closes the gap with Pyth for derivatives.
CCIP
A cross chain interoperability protocol that moves data and tokens across more than one network.
Exchange rate feeds
Price yield bearing collateral by asking the redemption rate and multiplying by the underlying price, rather than watching pool prices.
Chainlink · node operators behind a feed
09

The node operators behind a feed are visible on its page, each reporting and signing its own answer. data.chain.link/feeds

Chainlink · market pricing risk
10

Chainlink grades each feed by market pricing risk, about the market underneath the feed, not the oracle's uptime (Chainlink docs, selecting quality data feeds).

Low
Deep volume
Priced across many venues, hard to push around.
Medium
Thin or concentrated
Inconsistent volume, or sitting on one exchange.
High
Cross rate risk
Base trades mostly against something unpegged to the quote.
Very high
Distressed / new
Hacks, bridge failures, delistings, or newly launched tokens.

The things that make a feed risky, thin volume, concentration, cross rate exposure, are exactly what makes an asset dangerous to accept as collateral. The grade is a big part of a curator's listing decision.

Pyth · first party, pull model
11

The firms that make the prices, exchanges and trading firms, publish them directly. Prices are aggregated off chain, and consumers pull them on chain when needed, paying that update.

01
Publishers
Exchanges and trading firms sign and submit their own prices.
→
02
Oracle program
Runs on Pythnet, aggregates into a single value with a confidence interval.
→
03
Hermes
Serves the signed prices over an API.
→
04
Consumer
Fetches the latest price and submits it on chain.
Speed, ~400ms per update
Why Pyth is strong on Solana and other fast chains rather than EVM ones, and fits perpetual venues.
Confidence interval
A band showing how much publishers agree, so one bad price cannot drag the result far. Coverage extends to LSTs, equities, FX, metals.
RedStone · both models, one base
14

RedStone runs both push and pull, and the push is built on top of the pull. Data comes from many sources, CEXs, DEXs, and aggregators like CoinMarketCap or CoinGecko. Independent nodes combine them (median, TWAP, LWAP) and sign the result.

Filters before combining
Anomaly detection
Drops a price that jumps far from its recent trajectory.
Market depth
Checks liquidity behind a price, filters out thin venues.
Source variance
Throws out any source far from the median.
Peg monitoring
Flags pegged assets that drift abnormally.
Aggregation · median, LWAP, TWAP
15

Three ways to turn many raw prices into one robust number. Take five exchanges reporting ETH: 1,598, 1,600, 1,602, 1,604, and one outlier at 1,900. A plain average gives 1,661, dragged up by the outlier.

Median
Sort the five and take the middle one, 1,602. The 1,900 sits at the end and counts for nothing. Filters by position, across sources at one instant.
LWAP
Weight each source by liquidity. The 1,900 sits on a thin venue, so it barely counts and the weighted price lands near 1,601, essentially the deep venues on their own. Weights by market depth.
TWAP
Average over a time window. The price holds at 1,600 and spikes to 1,900 for one block out of thirty, so the average lands at 1,610, ten above the real price. To move it further you must hold the fake price the whole window. Smooths over time.

Same goal, a price that is robust and expensive to manipulate, on three different axes: median by position, LWAP by liquidity, TWAP by time.

RedStone · data flow
16

Left to right: data sources, oracle nodes, the Data Distribution Layer, consumers, and the chains it delivers to.

Oracle risks
17
ManipulationAlmost always via a flash loan that moves a thin market in one block, feeds the distorted price in, and repays. Polter Finance, 2025. Defense: source from many venues.
StalenessThe quieter risk. A push feed sits on an old price while the market moves. Defense: check the age of the price before acting on it.
Single provider dependencyThe risk underneath the others. Trust one feed with no cross check and any failure becomes the whole protocol's failure.

None of this means one provider is safe and the others are not. Picking a feed and reading its risk grade is a real decision for a lending market, not a formality.

Oracle risks · using more than one oracle
18

The defense against single provider dependency is to not rely on a single oracle at all. A multi oracle architecture layers a few feeds with different jobs.

Primary
Main feed
Carries the price, often Chainlink for an established lending market.
→
Fallback
Takes over
If the primary goes stale or deviates, usually a different provider so one bug does not take down both.
→
Breaker
Pauses
Compares the two and halts the protocol if they disagree beyond tolerance.

Euler and Liquity's later versions were built around exactly this. For a lending market, picking one provider is not enough. Oracle choice means a small system: a primary, a check, and a rule for what to do when they disagree.

What to take away
19
No universally best oracle
Chainlink for reliability, breadth, and integration depth. Pyth for speed and non-EVM reach. RedStone for cost, flexibility, and yield bearing assets.
Push vs pull is foundational
It splits by what the protocol is for. Lending favors push feeds it can read anytime, trading favors low latency pull.
Multi oracle is standard
One provider is a single point of failure. Serious protocols layer feeds with a fallback and a circuit breaker.

Where things are heading

OEV recapture turns the value that oracle updates create during liquidations from a leak into a revenue stream, which makes the oracle something that can pay for itself rather than a pure cost.
